title: Welcomed in
hookLine: the Ottoman sultan takes in refugees in Salonika and Istanbul

lines: STREETS THEY WILL NOT SEE AGAIN.
cards: Ships come into a crowded harbor at the far end of the Mediterranean. On board are families who have lost one home, and some of them a second.
They carry Spanish on their tongues, a few books, the names of streets they will never walk again. The question on every deck is the same: will anyone let us off this boat?
In the lands of the Ottoman sultan, the answer was yes. Today, welcomed in.

teach.b: The Ottoman sultan Bayezid the Second allowed the exiles from Spain to settle in his lands. They came to Istanbul, to Salonika, today's Thessaloniki in Greece, and to other port towns.
Tradition tells a story about him: that he said the king of Spain had made his own country poorer and the sultan's richer. Nobody can be sure he said it, but the story says something people believed.

The newcomers brought trades, printing presses, medicine and learning. What they found was not equality. Jews lived under the rules for non-Muslims, paid a special tax, and depended on the ruler's good will.

teach.h: NOT EQUAL, BUT FREE TO PRAY.
teach.b: But they could pray openly, keep their own courts and schools, and raise children as Jews. After Spain and Portugal, that was a great deal. Look at what they built.
In Salonika, congregations formed by home town, each keeping the customs of the city it came from, with names like Lisbon, Aragon and Catalonia.
Their Spanish became a Jewish language of its own, written in Hebrew letters, which we now call Ladino or Judeo-Spanish. The Torah gives the reason for welcome in plain words.

teach.h: YE KNOW THE HEART OF A STRANGER.
teach.b: In Exodus: "And a stranger shalt thou not oppress; for ye know the heart of a stranger, seeing ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." That verse speaks to Israel about strangers in its own land.
Here the roles were turned: the exiles were the strangers, and another people opened the gate. Being welcomed in did not erase what was lost. It made it possible to keep the rest.

how: Sephardic communities still keep customs, melodies and songs in Ladino that trace back to the exiles who settled in Ottoman lands, and Jewish law and teaching stress welcoming the stranger.

games.q: you are an exile arriving in Salonika. you can pray openly, but you pay a special tax and are not equal. what do you do?
o: sail on, looking for a place with full equality.
settle and build a congregation named for your home town.
games.why: the exiles settled and formed congregations by home town, keeping their customs and their Spanish.

practice: Remember your own first week somewhere new, a school, a job, a city, and what you didn't know yet that someone could have told you: where the bus stops, which shop is open late, who to ask.
Then bring to mind someone in that first week right now, perhaps someone who arrived from far away, and choose one practical thing you could hand them.

wordCard.voice: Welcomed in. The exiles from Spain settling in Ottoman lands, in Istanbul and Salonika, free to live openly as Jews and to keep the customs of their home towns. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: another people opened the gate. Not equal, but free to pray. See you tomorrow.
